teaching.h: Arabic reads right to left, and letters connect within a word
teaching.p: Unlike Latin script, Arabic is written right to left, and most letters change shape depending on whether they're at the start, middle, or end of a word — this is cursive joining, not decoration.
teaching.exTranslation: kitāb — book

teaching.h: 28 consonant letters, no separate uppercase
teaching.p: Arabic has 28 letters, all consonants (plus long vowels shown by certain letters). There's no uppercase/lowercase distinction like in English.
teaching.exTranslation: b, t, th — three letters that look almost identical, differing only by the number and position of dots

teaching.h: Short vowels are marks above/below the letter, often left out
teaching.p: Short vowels (a, i, u) are shown with small marks called tashkīl, placed above or below letters. Everyday newspapers and books usually omit them — native readers infer them from context.
teaching.exTranslation: kataba — he wrote (with vowel marks shown)

teaching.h: Long vowels are actual letters
teaching.p: Long vowels — ā, ī, ū — are written as full letters (ا, ي, و) rather than diacritics, so they're visible even in unvocalized text.
teaching.exTranslation: kitāb — book (the ا makes the long 'ā' sound)

quiz.q: Which word means 'book'?
Which word means 'pen'?
Type the Arabic word for 'house'.
Which word means 'school'?
Which word means 'door'?

teaching.h: Every noun is masculine or feminine
teaching.p: Arabic nouns are grammatically masculine or feminine — there's no neuter. Most feminine nouns end in ة (tāʼ marbūṭa), pronounced as a soft 'a'.
teaching.exTranslation: qalam (pen, m), madrasa (school, f)

teaching.h: The definite article ال doesn't change for gender or number
teaching.p: Unlike German's der/die/das, Arabic has just one definite article: ال (al-), prefixed directly onto the noun. It never changes, no matter the noun's gender or number.
teaching.exTranslation: al-kitāb — the book

teaching.h: No indefinite article — nunation marks 'a/an'
teaching.p: There's no separate word for 'a/an'. Instead, an extra 'n' sound (tanwīn) is added at the end of the indefinite noun, though it's usually silent in casual speech.
teaching.exTranslation: kitābun — a book (the ٌ mark shows indefinite nunation)

teaching.h: Definite vs indefinite changes the whole meaning of a sentence
teaching.p: Adding or dropping ال is one of the most important habits to build early — it distinguishes 'a book' from 'the book,' and later determines how adjectives and cases behave.
teaching.exTranslation: kitāb (a book) / al-kitāb (the book)

quiz.q: Which word is feminine (ends in ة)?
Which means 'the pen'?
Add the definite article to كتاب to say 'the book'.
Which means 'a school' (indefinite)?
Which word means 'the house'?

teaching.h: Arabic sentences often skip the verb 'to be' in the present
teaching.p: To say 'I am a student' or 'the book is new,' Arabic simply places two words side by side — no equivalent of 'am/is/are' is needed in the present tense.
teaching.exTranslation: anā ṭālib — I (am) a student

teaching.h: Personal pronouns for I, you, he, she
teaching.p: The core singular pronouns are أنا (I), أنتَ (you, m), أنتِ (you, f), هو (he/it), and هي (she/it) — Arabic distinguishes gender even in 'you.'
teaching.exTranslation: anta ṭālib (you, m, are a student), anti ṭāliba (you, f, are a student)

teaching.h: The subject can often be dropped, since the verb shows who's speaking
teaching.p: In verbal sentences, Arabic verbs are marked for person, so pronouns like أنا are often optional — the verb ending alone shows who's doing the action.
teaching.exTranslation: huwa mudarris — he (is) a teacher

teaching.h: Demonstratives: this / that also skip 'is'
teaching.p: هذا (this, m) and هذه (this, f) work the same way — just place them next to a noun, no verb needed.
teaching.exTranslation: hādhā kitāb — this (is) a book

quiz.q: Which means 'I am a teacher'?
Which pronoun means 'she'?
Complete: 'this is a book' → هذا ____
Which means 'you' (speaking to a woman)?
Which means 'he is a student'?

teaching.h: Present-tense verbs wrap the root with a prefix
teaching.p: Arabic present-tense verbs add a prefix (and sometimes a suffix) to a base root to show who's doing the action — no separate helping word like 'do' or 'am' is needed.
teaching.exTranslation: aktubu — I write

teaching.h: Different prefixes for I, you, he, she, we, they
teaching.p: The prefix changes with the subject: أ- (I), تـ- (you/she), يـ- (he/they-m). Once you know the pattern, you can conjugate almost any regular verb.
teaching.exTranslation: aktubu (I write), taktubu (you/she write(s)), yaktubu (he writes)

teaching.h: The same present form covers both 'write' and 'am writing'
teaching.p: Arabic doesn't separate simple present from present continuous the way English does — يَكْتُبُ can mean 'he writes' or 'he is writing,' depending on context.
teaching.exTranslation: huwa yaktubu risāla — he writes/is writing a letter

teaching.h: Negating the present with لا
teaching.p: To make a present-tense verb negative, just put لا directly before it.
teaching.exTranslation: lā afhamu — I don't understand

quiz.q: Which means 'I write'?
Which means 'he writes'?
Negate 'I understand' (أفهم) to say 'I don't understand'.
Which means 'she writes'?
Which sentence means 'he is writing a letter'?

teaching.h: Two sentence types: verbal and nominal
teaching.p: Arabic has verbal sentences (starting with a verb: Verb-Subject-Object) and nominal sentences (starting with a noun/pronoun, as in Unit 3). Both are completely normal — the choice shifts emphasis.
teaching.exTranslation: kataba aṭ-ṭālibu ad-darsa — the student wrote the lesson (verb first)

teaching.h: Verb-Subject-Object is the 'default' word order
teaching.p: Unlike English's Subject-Verb-Object, formal Arabic often puts the verb first, then the subject, then the object — though spoken Arabic frequently uses S-V-O too.
teaching.exTranslation: yashrabu al-waladu al-ḥalība — the boy drinks the milk (drinks-boy-milk)

teaching.h: Adjectives come after the noun, not before
teaching.p: Unlike English, descriptive adjectives follow the noun they describe, and must match it in gender, number, and definiteness (more on this in a later lesson).
teaching.exTranslation: baytun kabīrun — a big house (literally: house big)

teaching.h: Questions often just add a question word to a normal sentence
teaching.p: You can frequently turn a statement into a question just by adding a question word at the front — sentence order otherwise stays the same.
teaching.exTranslation: hal tafhamu? — do you understand?

quiz.q: In 'the boy drinks the milk,' which Arabic word comes first?
Which is grammatically correct for 'a big house'?
Turn 'you understand' (تفهم) into a question meaning 'do you understand?'
Which sentence follows Verb-Subject-Object order?
Which means 'a big house'?

teaching.h: The ل in ال sometimes disappears in pronunciation
teaching.p: Arabic letters split into two groups: sun letters (14) and moon letters (14). Before a sun letter, the ل of ال is silent and the following consonant doubles instead.
teaching.exTranslation: ash-shams — the sun (ل is silent, ش doubles — a sun letter, fittingly)

teaching.h: Before moon letters, ال is pronounced normally
teaching.p: Moon letters keep the ل sound exactly as written — no assimilation happens.
teaching.exTranslation: al-qamar — the moon

teaching.h: Spelling never changes — only pronunciation does
teaching.p: This is purely a pronunciation rule. Whether a word starts with a sun or moon letter, ال is always written the same way — you just say it differently.
teaching.exTranslation: ar-rajul (the man, sun letter ر) / al-kitāb (the book, moon letter ك) — both spelled with ال

teaching.h: A doubling mark (shadda) shows the assimilation in vocalized text
teaching.p: In fully vocalized writing, a small ّ (shadda) sits over the doubled sun letter, showing it's pronounced twice as long — the trace of the missing ل sound.
teaching.exTranslation: an-nahār — the daytime

quiz.q: Which is a sun letter word (ل is silent)?
Which is a moon letter word (ل is pronounced)?
How is 'الرجل' (the man) pronounced — write the transliteration starting with 'ar-'.
Does the spelling of ال change before sun letters?
Which word correctly means 'the daytime'?

teaching.h: Adjectives must match their noun in gender
teaching.p: If the noun is feminine, the adjective typically gets a ة ending too — even if the adjective wouldn't normally look feminine on its own.
teaching.exTranslation: waladun ṣaghīr (a small boy), bintun ṣaghīra (a small girl)

teaching.h: Adjectives must also match definiteness
teaching.p: If the noun has ال, the adjective needs ال too — dropping it on just one side is a common learner mistake.
teaching.exTranslation: al-waladu aṣ-ṣaghīru — the small boy (both noun and adjective take ال)

teaching.h: Word order: noun first, then adjective
teaching.p: As covered earlier, the adjective always follows its noun. This never flips, even in questions or negative sentences.
teaching.exTranslation: baytun jamīl — a beautiful house

teaching.h: Non-human plurals take FEMININE SINGULAR adjectives
teaching.p: This one surprises a lot of learners: plural nouns for objects/animals (not people) are grammatically treated as feminine singular for agreement purposes.
teaching.exTranslation: kutubun jadīda — new books (jadīda is feminine singular, even though 'books' is plural)

quiz.q: Which correctly matches 'a small girl'?
Which correctly says 'the beautiful house' (both definite)?
Make 'صغير' (small) agree with the feminine noun بنت.
Which correctly describes 'new books' (non-human plural)?
Which means 'a small boy'?

teaching.h: Arabic has no separate word for 'of' — nouns just sit next to each other
teaching.p: To say 'the student's book' or 'book of the student,' Arabic places two nouns back-to-back. This pairing is called iḍāfa (addition).
teaching.exTranslation: kitābu aṭ-ṭālibi — the student's book (literally: book-of the-student)

teaching.h: Only the second noun takes ال — never the first
teaching.p: In an iḍāfa, the definite article only ever goes on the LAST word. The first noun (the 'possessed' item) never takes ال, even though the whole phrase is understood as definite.
teaching.exTranslation: baytu al-mudarrisi — the teacher's house (بيت never gets ال here)

teaching.h: Longer chains just keep stacking
teaching.p: You can chain more than two nouns together — 'the door of the house of the teacher' — and the same rule holds: only the very last noun takes ال.
teaching.exTranslation: bābu bayti al-mudarrisi — the door of the teacher's house

teaching.h: Pronoun suffixes are a shortcut for 'my/your/his/her'
teaching.p: Instead of a full second noun, you can attach a pronoun suffix directly to the first noun to mean 'my book,' 'your book,' etc.
teaching.exTranslation: kitābī (my book), kitābuka (your book, m), kitābuhu (his book)

quiz.q: Which correctly means 'the student's book'?
Which correctly follows the idafa rule (only last noun gets ال)?
Say 'my book' using a pronoun suffix on كتاب.
Which means 'his house'?
Which correctly means 'the door of the house'?

teaching.h: Sound masculine plural: add ون or ين
teaching.p: For most masculine words describing people, add ون (subject position) or ين (object/after preposition) to the end.
teaching.exTranslation: mudarris (teacher) → mudarrisūn (teachers)

teaching.h: Sound feminine plural: swap ة for ات
teaching.p: For most feminine words, just change the ة ending to ات.
teaching.exTranslation: mudarrisa (teacher, f) → mudarrisāt (teachers, f)

teaching.h: Broken plurals change the internal pattern — and must be memorized
teaching.p: Most non-human nouns (and many human ones) form plurals by changing the internal vowel pattern entirely, not by adding an ending. There's no shortcut — each noun's broken plural is learned individually.
teaching.exTranslation: kitāb (book) → kutub (books) — completely different internal pattern

teaching.h: Broken plurals act as feminine singular for agreement (recap)
teaching.p: As covered in the adjectives lesson, broken plurals for non-human nouns are treated as grammatically feminine singular — this connects directly back to that rule.
teaching.exTranslation: buyūtun kabīra — big houses (buyūt is the broken plural of bayt)

quiz.q: What's the plural of مدرس (teacher, m)?
What's the plural of مدرسة (teacher, f)?
Give the broken plural of كتاب (book).
Which is the correct plural of بيت (house)?
Which agreement is correct for a broken plural noun?

teaching.h: Arabic has a special form just for exactly two
teaching.p: Beyond singular and plural, Arabic has a third number: the dual, used for exactly two of something. It's not optional — using plural for two items sounds wrong.
teaching.exTranslation: kitābāni — two books

teaching.h: Form the dual by adding ان (or ين)
teaching.p: Add ان to the singular noun for the subject position, or ين elsewhere in the sentence — this mirrors the masculine sound plural's ون/ين pattern.
teaching.exTranslation: ṭālibāni (two students, subject) / ṭālibayni (two students, object)

teaching.h: Feminine nouns keep their ة before the dual ending
teaching.p: A feminine noun's ة becomes ت before the dual ending is added, since ة only appears at the very end of a word.
teaching.exTranslation: mudarrisatāni — two (female) teachers

teaching.h: Dual verbs and pronouns exist too
teaching.p: It's not just nouns — Arabic also has dual pronouns (أنتما, هما) and matching dual verb endings, though many learners meet noun duals first.
teaching.exTranslation: humā ṭālibāni — the two of them (are) students

quiz.q: How do you say 'two books'?
Which correctly means 'two (female) teachers'?
Give the dual form of طالب (student) for the subject position.
Which pronoun means 'the two of them'?
Which correctly means '(the) two of them are students'?

teaching.h: Past tense uses suffixes instead of prefixes
teaching.p: Unlike the present tense's prefixes, the past tense attaches a suffix to the verb root to show who did the action.
teaching.exTranslation: katabtu — I wrote

teaching.h: The base 'he' form has no suffix at all
teaching.p: The third-person masculine singular ('he') is the bare root with no ending added — it's the form dictionaries list verbs under.
teaching.exTranslation: kataba — he wrote

teaching.h: Different suffixes for I, you, she, we, they
teaching.p: تُ marks 'I,' تَ marks 'you (m),' تْ marks 'she,' نَا marks 'we' — memorizing this suffix set unlocks the whole past tense for regular verbs.
teaching.exTranslation: katabta (you, m, wrote), katabat (she wrote), katabnā (we wrote)

teaching.h: Negate the past with ما, not لا
teaching.p: While لا negates the present tense, ما is used to negate the past — a small but important switch.
teaching.exTranslation: mā katabtu — I did not write

quiz.q: Which means 'I wrote'?
Which means 'she wrote'?
Negate 'كتبتُ' (I wrote) using ما to say 'I did not write'.
Which is the bare dictionary form, meaning 'he wrote'?
Which means 'we wrote'?

teaching.h: Different negation words for different tenses
teaching.p: Arabic doesn't use one all-purpose 'not' — لا negates the present, ما negates the past, and لن negates the future. Picking the right one matters.
teaching.ex: لَا أَعْرِفُ، مَا عَرَفْتُ، لَنْ أَعْرِفَ
teaching.exTranslation: lā aʻrifu (I don't know), mā ʻaraftu (I didn't know), lan aʻrifa (I won't know)

teaching.h: لم + jussive is a more formal way to negate the past
teaching.p: Formal/written Arabic often prefers لم followed by a special present-tense form (the jussive) instead of ما — both mean 'did not,' but لم is more common in writing.
teaching.exTranslation: lam afham — I did not understand

teaching.h: Negating nominal (noun) sentences uses ليس
teaching.p: For 'is not / are not' in equational sentences (no verb), Arabic uses the special word ليس, which itself conjugates like a past-tense verb.
teaching.exTranslation: huwa laysa ṭāliban — he is not a student

teaching.h: لن always signals the future, and takes the subjunctive
teaching.p: لن exclusively negates future actions and requires the subjunctive verb form (a slightly different present-tense ending) — a nice giveaway that 'won't' is coming.
teaching.exTranslation: lan adhhaba — I will not go

quiz.q: Which negates a present-tense verb?
Which negates a past-tense verb (simple form)?
Negate 'أذهب' (I go) to mean 'I will not go', using لن + subjunctive.
Which word negates a nominal (verbless) sentence, like 'he is not...'?
Which is the more formal way to negate the past, using the jussive?

teaching.h: Yes/no questions: just add هل or أ to the front
teaching.p: To turn any statement into a yes/no question, add هل (or the shorter أ) right at the start — the rest of the sentence stays exactly the same.
teaching.exTranslation: hal anta ṭālib? — are you a student?

teaching.h: مَن asks 'who,' مَا/مَاذا asks 'what'
teaching.p: مَن is for people ('who'), while مَا (before nouns) or مَاذا (before verbs) is for things ('what'). Mixing these up is one of the most common early mistakes.
teaching.exTranslation: man hādhā? (who is this?) mā hādhā? (what is this?)

teaching.h: أَيْنَ (where), مَتَى (when), كَيْفَ (how), لِمَاذَا (why)
teaching.p: These four question words work at the front of a sentence just like English, no special word order changes needed.
teaching.exTranslation: ayna al-baytu? — where is the house?

teaching.h: كَمْ (how many) is followed by a singular noun, not a plural
teaching.p: This one trips up learners: after كم, the counted noun stays singular and takes an accusative ending — it feels backwards coming from English.
teaching.exTranslation: kam kitāban? — how many books? (kitāb stays singular)

quiz.q: Which word turns a statement into a yes/no question?
Which word means 'who'?
Ask 'where is the house?' starting with أين.
Which word means 'how many'?
Which word means 'why'?

teaching.h: Prepositions always pull the noun after them into the genitive
teaching.p: Any noun following a preposition takes a special ending called the genitive case (usually a kasra, or -i sound) — one of the most reliable case rules in Arabic.
teaching.exTranslation: fī al-bayti — in the house

teaching.h: في (in), على (on), إلى (to), مِن (from)
teaching.p: These four cover most everyday situations and are worth memorizing as a set early on.
teaching.exTranslation: mina al-madrasati ilā al-bayti — from the school to the house

teaching.h: مَعَ (with) and عِنْدَ (at/have) are especially common
teaching.p: عِنْدَ is worth special attention: it's also how Arabic expresses 'to have' — literally 'at me (is) a book' for 'I have a book.'
teaching.exTranslation: ʻindī kitāb — I have a book (literally: at-me a book)

teaching.h: Prepositions combine with pronoun suffixes too
teaching.p: Just like the idafa construction, pronoun suffixes attach directly onto prepositions instead of needing a separate word.
teaching.exTranslation: maʻī (with me), maʻaka (with you, m), maʻahu (with him)

quiz.q: Which means 'in the house'?
Which preposition means 'from'?
Say 'I have a book' using عند + a pronoun suffix.
Which means 'with him'?
Which means 'to the school'?

teaching.h: Three cases: nominative, accusative, genitive
teaching.p: Formal Arabic marks a noun's grammatical role with a short vowel case ending: -u for the subject (nominative), -a for the direct object (accusative), and -i after a preposition or in idafa (genitive).
teaching.exTranslation: al-waladu (the boy, subject) / al-walada (the boy, object) / al-waladi (the boy, after preposition/in idafa)

teaching.h: These endings are almost always silent in speech
teaching.p: In everyday spoken Arabic, and even careful reading of unvocalized text, these case vowels are usually dropped. They matter most for formal recitation and grammatical analysis.
teaching.exTranslation: al-waladu yaktubu ad-darsa — the boy writes the lesson (subject -u, object -a marked)

teaching.h: Indefinite nouns double the case vowel (nunation), recap
teaching.p: As covered back in Unit 2, indefinite nouns add an 'n' sound to the case ending — waladun (a boy, subject), waladan (a boy, object), waladin (a boy, genitive).
teaching.exTranslation: waladun / waladan / waladin — a boy, in the three cases

teaching.h: Sound plurals use different, easier-to-spot case endings
teaching.p: Instead of short vowels, sound masculine plurals switch their whole ending: ون for nominative, ين for accusative/genitive — visible even without diacritics.
teaching.exTranslation: al-mudarrisūna (the teachers, subject) / al-mudarrisīna (the teachers, object/genitive)

quiz.q: Which form of 'the boy' is correctly marked as the subject?
Which form correctly marks 'the boy' as a direct object?
Give the genitive (after a preposition) form of الولد.
Which is the correct indefinite accusative of ولد (a boy, as object)?
Which is the correct nominative plural of مدرس (teachers, subject)?

teaching.h: Numbers 1 and 2 act like adjectives, agreeing with the noun
teaching.p: واحد (one) and اثنان (two) come AFTER the noun and agree in gender, just like a regular adjective — though for 'two,' the dual form alone is usually enough without adding اثنان.
teaching.exTranslation: waladun wāḥid (one boy), bintāni (two girls — dual form alone)

teaching.h: Numbers 3–10 flip gender and take a plural noun
teaching.p: Here's the famous curveball: numbers 3 through 10 show the OPPOSITE gender of the noun they count, and the noun that follows is plural and genitive.
teaching.exTranslation: thalāthatu kutubin — three books (kutub is grammatically masculine, so the number takes the feminine form thalātha)

teaching.h: Numbers 11–99 take a singular accusative noun
teaching.p: Once you pass ten, the counted noun switches back to singular, now marked accusative — different again from both the 1–2 and 3–10 patterns.
teaching.exTranslation: ʻishrūna kitāban — twenty books (kitāb stays singular, accusative)

teaching.h: أَوَّل (first), ثَانِي (second)... ordinals work like adjectives too
teaching.p: Ordinal numbers behave like regular adjectives — placed after the noun, agreeing in gender and definiteness.
teaching.exTranslation: ad-darsu al-awwalu — the first lesson

quiz.q: Which correctly means 'one boy'?
Which correctly means 'three books' (3-10 rule)?
Give the ordinal 'first' as it agrees with الدرس (the lesson, m, definite).
Which correctly means 'twenty books' (11-99 rule, singular accusative)?
Which correctly means 'two girls' using the dual form alone?
